1.open: Think of a time someone dropped everything to help you or show up for you. What did they do?
questions: John's message was "a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins," and people came "confessing their sins" (vv. 4, 5). Why might it take courage to name our wrongs out loud, and what makes it easier?
At his baptism a voice says, "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased" (v. 11). This comes before Jesus has done any public work. What does it mean to you that approval can come first?
Verse 12 says the Spirit "drove Jesus into the wilderness," where he was tempted. Why do you think a hard season might follow a high moment? Have you seen that in your own life?

Jesus says, "The time is fulfilled," and "the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!" (v. 15). In your own words, what is he inviting people to do? Christians differ on whether this kingdom is mainly here now, still to come, or both. What do you make of that?
Simon and Andrew "at once" left their nets, and James and John left their father in the boat (vv. 18, 20). What would following Jesus have cost them? What might it ask of us, even in ordinary life?
The people were astonished because Jesus "taught as one who had authority" (v. 22). What makes someone's words carry real weight with you, beyond their title or training?
After a night of healing, Jesus went to "a solitary place to pray" while everyone was looking for him (vv. 35, 37). What does he choose here, and what pulls you away from quiet or prayer?

A man with leprosy says, "If You are willing, You can make me clean," and Jesus answers, "I am willing" (vv. 40, 41). He also touched him. If you were honest, where do you find it hard to believe Jesus is willing to help you? Say as much or as little as you like.
1.life: Jesus made room to pray before the day got loud. This week, pick one short, regular time, even ten minutes, to be quiet with God before your day fills up. Notice what changes.
1.prayer: Thank God that Jesus came near and was willing. Ask for honesty about where we need to turn back to him, and for ears to hear his call to follow.
1.tip: The spirit-driving-out scenes (vv. 23-27, 34) can feel strange or unsettling to some. You do not need to explain them fully. Point to what the people notice: Jesus has real authority and uses it to free people. Keep the focus there, and let a doubtful person say it feels odd without rushing to fix it.

2.open: Who is someone who went out of their way to help you, even when it was inconvenient for them?
questions: The four friends could not get through the crowd, so they "uncovered the roof above Him" (v. 4). What does their effort tell you about how much they cared for their friend, and who has carried you at a hard time?
Jesus' first words to the man are "Son, your sins are forgiven" (v. 5), not a word about walking. Why do you think he started there? What would you have expected him to say?
The scribes ask, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (v. 7). They had a point. What is Jesus claiming about himself when he forgives sins, and how did the healing back up that claim (v. 10)?

Jesus invites Levi, a tax collector, with just two words, "Follow Me" (v. 14). Why might someone like Levi have found that hard to believe, and what would make it hard for you to believe an invitation like that?

Jesus says, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick" (v. 17). Why can it be hard to admit we are the ones who need help? Answer as honestly as you can, including if you are unsure where you stand with God.

In verses 21 and 22 Jesus talks about new patches and new wineskins. Christians read these pictures in different ways, but most agree they point to something fresh that does not fit neatly into old habits. Where do you see tension between what is familiar and what Jesus is doing?
Jesus says, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" (v. 27). When have you seen a rule or tradition help people, and when have you seen it get in the way of someone who needed help?

Jesus claims the Son of Man is "Lord even of the Sabbath" (v. 28). Christians disagree about what that means for a weekly day of rest today. How do you practice rest, and what would real rest look like for you?
2.life: Pick one person who seems to be on the outside of things, at work, school or in your street. This week, share a meal or a coffee with them, with no agenda beyond welcome. Also set aside one stretch of real rest, and notice it as a gift.
2.prayer: Thank Jesus that he forgives and that he welcomes people who know they need him. Ask for friends who will carry us, and for the willingness to carry others.
2.tip: Verses 21 and 22 and the Sabbath question can pull the group into long debates. Say plainly that Christians read these differently, then steer back to what is clear: Jesus forgives, welcomes the needy, and cares more about people than about rules. Give quiet members space for question 5 without putting anyone on the spot.

3.open: Think of a time when a crowd, a family gathering or a group of friends got so busy that nobody had time to eat or rest. What happened?
questions: The religious leaders were "watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath" so they could accuse him (v. 2). What do you think it does to a person to watch others only to catch them out?

Jesus asks, "Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?" and they are silent (v. 4). Why might they have stayed silent, and when have you stayed silent when you should have spoken?
Verse 5 says Jesus looked at them "with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart." What does it tell you that Jesus feels both anger and sorrow at the same moment?

Jesus "called for those He wanted, and they came to Him" (v. 13), and the list of twelve includes "Sons of Thunder" and "Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus" (vv. 17, 19). What does it say about Jesus that he chose such a mixed group?
His own family said, "He is out of His mind" (v. 21). Have you ever been doubted or misunderstood by people close to you? What did that feel like, and how did you respond?
Jesus says a house "divided against itself" cannot stand (v. 25). Where have you seen division wear down a family, a church or a friendship?

Jesus says "whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven" (v. 29). Christians differ on exactly what this means. If this verse has ever worried you, what would you like to say or ask about it?
Jesus says, "whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother" (v. 35). Who has been like family to you in faith, and how could you be that for someone else?
3.life: Think of one person who seems on the edge of your group, church or circle of friends. This week, invite them to share a meal or a conversation, and treat them as family.
3.prayer: Thank God that Jesus welcomes all who come to him, including people who are doubted or misunderstood. Ask for eyes to see who needs a place at the table, and for honesty to bring your own doubts to him.
3.tip: Verses 28 and 29 may frighten someone in the room who fears they have done something unforgivable. Say plainly that Christians understand this passage differently, point out that Mark ties it to people calling God's work evil, and note that a person troubled about it is usually not the person Jesus was describing. Invite anyone still worried to talk with you or a pastor afterwards.

4.open: Have you ever planted anything, even a houseplant, and been surprised by how it turned out?
questions: Jesus begins with "Listen!" and ends the story with "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (vv. 3, 9). What do you think it takes to really hear something, and not just let it pass by?
Farmers then scattered seed by hand, so some of it was bound to land on bad ground. What does it tell you that Jesus pictures a farmer who sows generously, even where much will be lost?
Jesus names four kinds of soil: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns and the good soil (vv. 15 to 20). Which one best describes you right now, and what has shaped it?

Some people receive the word "with joy" but "have no root" and fall away when "trouble or persecution" comes (vv. 16, 17). Why do you think hard times test faith so sharply? Have you seen that in your own life or someone else's?

Verse 19 lists "the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things." Which of these tends to crowd out your attention to God, and what does that look like on an ordinary week?

In verses 11 and 12 Jesus quotes Isaiah about people "ever seeing but never perceiving." Christians read this differently: some think Jesus used stories on purpose to keep some people from understanding, others think stories simply reveal who is truly listening. How does each reading sound to you, and what questions does it raise?

In the stories of the growing seed and the mustard seed, the kingdom grows quietly and starts small (vv. 27, 31, 32). Where in your life or church are you tempted to want faster or bigger results? What would it look like to trust God with the growing?

In the storm the disciples cry, "Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?" (v. 38). Have you ever felt that God was asleep while you were struggling? Say it as honestly as you can, whether or not you feel you have an answer.
4.life: This week, pick one time each day to slow down and read a few verses with no distractions. Afterward, ask yourself which kind of soil you were that day, and tell God honestly what you noticed.
4.prayer: Ask God to soften the ground of your heart so his word can take root. Pray also for anyone in the group who is in a storm right now and wondering whether God cares.
4.tip: Verses 11 and 12 are confusing, and people may get stuck on them. Say once that Christians read them differently, then steer back to Jesus' explanation in verses 14 to 20. Also, when people name which soil they are, avoid labeling anyone. Jesus gives the story as an invitation to grow, not a verdict.

5.open: Who is the first person you call when something goes wrong, and why them?
questions: Verses 3 to 5 describe a man no one could hold, who "kept crying out and cutting himself with stones" (v. 5). What do you think life was like for him, and for the people around him?

Christians read this story differently. Some see literal evil spirits, and others see a severe illness described in the language of that time. However you read it, what does the story show about how Jesus treats someone everyone else has given up on?

The townspeople saw the man "clothed and in his right mind," yet they "were afraid" and began to "beg Jesus to leave their region" (vv. 15, 17). Why might people feel uneasy instead of relieved when someone's life changes in a way they can't explain?
The healed man wanted to go with Jesus, but Jesus said, "Go home to your own people" (v. 19). Why might Jesus have given him that job instead? Who is your own people, and what would you tell them?

The woman had suffered for twelve years and spent all she had, and she told herself, "If only I touch His garments, I will be healed" (v. 28). Where have you tried a lot of things and still feel stuck? What do you do with that?

Jesus stopped and kept looking for her. She "told Him the whole truth," and He called her "Daughter" (vv. 32 to 34). Why might it matter that Jesus did more than heal her quietly and let her slip away?

Jairus has just heard that his daughter is dead, and Jesus says, "Do not be afraid; just believe" (v. 36). What do you think that asked of him? Which part of this chapter is hardest for you to take in, and what would you honestly want to ask Jesus about it?
5.life: Think of one way God has shown you mercy, big or small. This week, tell one person about it in a sentence or two, the way the man in verse 19 was sent to do.
5.prayer: Thank Jesus that He notices people others avoid, overlook or give up on. Ask Him to meet anyone in the group who feels stuck, afraid or worn out from waiting.
5.tip: People will likely get stuck on the pigs or on whether the first story is literal possession. Say plainly that Christians disagree and that the story itself gives no reason for the pigs, then steer back to what Jesus does for the people in the chapter. Leave room for doubt, and let someone say 'I find this hard to believe' without anyone rushing to fix it.

6.open: Think of a place where people still remember you as you were at ten years old. What do they still tease you about?
questions: The people in Nazareth asked, "Isn't this the carpenter?" (v. 3). Why might it be hard to take someone seriously when you already know their family and where they came from?
Mark says Jesus "was amazed at their unbelief" (v. 6). What do you make of the fact that Jesus could be surprised, and that so little happened there?

Jesus sent the Twelve out with "nothing but a staff" (v. 8). What would it feel like to head out with so little? What do you tend to pack, in a literal or personal sense, so you will not have to depend on anyone?
Herod "feared John" and "listened to him gladly," yet still had him killed (vv. 20, 27). How does a person end up so close to the truth and still act against it?
John's story ends in a prison and a tomb, with no rescue (vv. 27-29). If you have ever wondered where God is when good people suffer, what would you want to say about that here?

When Jesus saw the crowd, "He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd" (v. 34). Who around you seems to be without care or direction, and what do you notice about how Jesus responds to them?

Jesus told the disciples, "You give them something to eat," and all they had was "Five, and two fish" (vv. 37, 38). What is a need in front of you right now that feels bigger than what you have to offer?

Mark says the disciples were astounded, "for they had not understood about the loaves" (v. 52). Where do you find yourself still not quite getting who Jesus is, and what would an honest answer sound like?
6.life: Pick one small thing you have, like an hour, a meal, a phone call or a skill, and hand it over to someone in need this week. Ask God to make it enough, and notice what happens.
6.prayer: Thank Jesus for seeing the crowds and the lonely with compassion. Ask him to help you offer what little you have, and to be patient with the parts of him you do not yet understand.
6.tip: The death of John (vv. 14-29) can stop a group cold, and someone may ask why God lets this happen. Do not rush to explain it. Let the passage stand as the hard story it is, name that Mark gives no tidy answer, and then notice together that Jesus goes on caring for the crowds. Also note that Christians differ on whether the feeding and the walk on the lake are meant mainly as literal miracles or as symbolic stories about who Jesus is. Say so in one line and keep the focus on what the text shows about him.

7.open: What is a rule or habit from your family growing up that you still follow, even if you can't quite say why?
questions: The Pharisees ask why the disciples ignore "the tradition of the elders" (v. 5). What were they really concerned about, and why might it have felt important to them?
Jesus quotes Isaiah: "These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me" (v. 6). When can religious words or habits drift away from what is going on inside us?

In the Corban example, a religious vow was used to avoid caring for parents (vv. 10-12). What would that have meant for an aging mother or father, and what are modern ways of using a good reason to dodge a plain duty?

Jesus says, "Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him" (v. 15). What did that mean to people who had kept careful purity rules all their lives, and how might it sound to someone who feels they are not good enough for God?

Verses 21 and 22 list what comes "from within the hearts of men," from theft and murder to envy and arrogance. Which of these is easiest to hide from other people, and what do you think Jesus offers someone who sees it in themselves?

A Greek mother keeps asking for her daughter, and Jesus' first answer sounds harsh (vv. 26-27). Scholars disagree about his tone. What do you notice about her reply in verse 28, and what do you make of the way the conversation turns out?

The crowd says of the deaf man's healing, "He has done all things well!" (v. 37). Is there an area of your life where you find that hard to say right now? Be as honest as you like, including if the honest answer is that you aren't sure.
Both healings happen in largely non-Jewish regions. What does it tell you about who Jesus came for, and who might we be tempted to leave outside?
7.life: This week, pick one habit or rule you follow in your faith and ask yourself what it is meant to point to. Then do one small, concrete thing that serves a real person, such as calling a parent or an older neighbor.
7.prayer: Ask God to look past your words and rules and meet you in your heart. Pray for anyone in the group who feels far away from God or left out.
7.tip: Verses 18 and 19 touch on food laws, and Christians disagree about whether Jesus himself set those laws aside or whether that was a later conclusion. Name that in a sentence and move on. Keep the group on verse 15 and the heart. Also, the woman's exchange with Jesus can unsettle people, so let them say it sounds hard without rushing to explain it away.

8.open: Think of a time you misunderstood something obvious, like a joke, a set of directions or what someone really meant. What happened?
questions: Jesus says, "I have compassion for this crowd" (v. 2). What does it tell you about him that he noticed their hunger before anyone asked?
The disciples ask, "Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?" (v. 4). Have you ever faced a need that felt far too big? What did you do with it?
The Pharisees demanded "a sign from heaven" (v. 11), and Jesus "sighed deeply in His spirit" (v. 12). Why do you think he refused, and what does his sigh suggest about how he felt?
Jesus asks the disciples, "Do you still not see or understand?" (v. 17). What do you think they were missing about him, even after two feedings?

The blind man needed a second touch before he could "see everything clearly" (v. 25). Many readers see this as a picture of the disciples. Where would you say your own understanding of Jesus is blurry right now? Honest answers, including doubts, are welcome here.
Jesus asks, "Who do you say I am?" (v. 29). How would you answer in your own words, not the answer you think you should give?
Peter is right that Jesus is the Christ, yet he rebukes Jesus for talking about suffering (vv. 29-32). Why might a good answer about Jesus still miss what Jesus came to do?
Jesus says, "whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it" (v. 35). What do you think he means, and what might following him cost people in our setting today?
8.life: Each day this week, ask yourself Jesus' question, "Who do you say I am?" Write down one honest sentence in answer, and one place where you could follow him more closely.
8.prayer: Ask Jesus to open the eyes of the group so they see him more clearly. Pray for honesty about doubts, and for courage to follow him when it costs something.
8.tip: Verses 34 to 38 can feel heavy, and some people may hear them as pressure or as a call to seek out suffering. Keep the focus on Jesus going first and on his compassion in the opening verses, and let quiet people answer the question about who Jesus is at their own pace.

9.open: When did you last have a moment you wished you could freeze and stay in for good?
questions: Peter was so frightened that he "did not know what else to say" (v. 6), so he offered to build shelters. Why do you think we try to hold on to great spiritual moments, and what happens when we can't?
The voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!" (v. 7). What do you think it means to listen to Jesus, and what makes that hard in a noisy week?
The father says, "if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us" (v. 22). What does his situation tell you about how long he had been carrying this, and about why he spoke the way he did?
He answers Jesus with, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (v. 24). Where in your own life do trust and doubt sit side by side? Be as honest as you like, including saying you aren't sure.
Jesus takes the boy "by the hand" and helps him to his feet (v. 27). What does that small detail show you about Jesus?

Right after Jesus speaks about his death, the disciples are arguing about "which of them was the greatest" (v. 34). Where do you see that same pull toward rank or comparison in our workplaces, churches or families?

Jesus says, "If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all" (v. 35), and he puts a child in the middle of the room. Who plays that role in your world, the person easy to overlook, and what would welcoming them look like?

John wanted to stop someone because "he does not accompany us" (v. 38). Jesus says, "whoever is not against us is for us" (v. 40). How do we decide who counts as one of us, and how does this challenge that?
9.life: Pick one person who is easy to overlook, such as a new neighbor, a lonely coworker or a child you know. This week, give them real time and attention, as a small way of welcoming them in Jesus' name.
9.prayer: Bring God an honest mix of trust and doubt, using the father's words, "help my unbelief." Ask for a servant's heart and for help welcoming the people we tend to pass by.
9.tip: Verses 43 to 48 about cutting off a hand and about hell can pull the whole meeting into a debate. Note that many readers take the hand and eye language as deliberate exaggeration about taking sin seriously, and that Christians differ on how to understand hell and on what verse 1 means. Then bring the group back to the father's honest prayer and the child in the middle. If you have time, you can mention that the salt sayings in verses 49 and 50 are hard to pin down.

10.open: Who is someone who made you feel welcome the first time you walked into a room full of strangers?
questions: The disciples tried to send the children away, and Jesus was "indignant" (v. 14). Why do you think the disciples saw the children as a bother, and what does Jesus' reaction show you about him?
Jesus says we must receive the kingdom of God "like a little child" (v. 15). What do you think that looks like for an adult who is used to earning things?
The man asks, "what must I do to inherit eternal life?" (v. 17). Why might a good, sincere person still be asking that question? Have you ever wondered whether you have done enough?
Mark says Jesus "looked at him, loved him" before asking him to give up everything (v. 21). How does it change the way you hear the request to know it came from love?

Christians differ on whether Jesus' call to sell everything is meant for every follower or was a specific test for this one man. What do you think holds you back from following Jesus fully, whether money or something else?

When the disciples ask, "Who then can be saved?" Jesus answers, "With man this is impossible, but not with God" (vv. 26, 27). Where do you find that comforting, and where do you find it hard to trust?

James and John ask for seats of honor right after Jesus describes his death. Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (v. 43). Where do you see the world's way of measuring greatness creeping into our own thinking?
Jesus asks both James and John and Bartimaeus, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (vv. 36, 51). What would you honestly say if he asked you tonight, even if your answer feels small or uncertain?
10.life: Jesus said he came "to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (v. 45). This week, choose one quiet act of service that no one will notice or thank you for, and do it. Then notice how it feels.
10.prayer: Thank Jesus for coming to serve and to give his life for us. Ask him to show you what you most want from him, and to loosen your grip on anything that keeps you from following him.
10.tip: The rich man and the camel verses can leave people anxious or defensive about money. Gently point the group to verse 27: the passage ends with what God can do, not with a guilt trip. Let people answer honestly about their own struggles without comparing or judging each other.

11.open: What is something you lent to someone, or borrowed, and never quite got back or gave back?
questions: Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a colt and tells them to say, "The Lord needs it" (v. 3). What does it say about Jesus that he asks to borrow something, and what might he be asking to borrow from you?

The crowd spreads cloaks and branches and shouts, "Hosanna!" (vv. 8, 9). Riding a young donkey recalled an old promise of a humble king. What kind of king were people hoping for, and what kind did they get?
In verse 13 Jesus finds "nothing on it except leaves." When have you seen something that looked impressive from a distance but was empty up close, whether in a place, a group or yourself?

Jesus says the temple was meant to be "a house of prayer for all the nations" but had become "a den of robbers" (v. 17). The market sat in the court where non-Jews were meant to pray. What can crowd out the people God wants welcomed in a church today?

Christians differ on whether Jesus was calling for the temple to be reformed, or signaling that the whole temple system was coming to an end. What do you notice in the text that leans you one way or the other, or leaves you unsure?

Jesus says, "Have faith in God" and talks about a mountain being moved (vv. 22, 23). How do you honestly feel when you read his words about prayer in verse 24? Is it hope, confusion, frustration, or something else?
Right after teaching on prayer, Jesus says, "if you hold anything against another, forgive it" (v. 25). Why might he connect forgiving others with praying to God? What makes that hard?

The leaders ask, "By what authority are You doing these things?" and then say, "We do not know" because they fear the crowd (vv. 28, 33). When have you given a vague answer because the honest one felt costly?
11.life: Think of one person you have been holding something against. This week, bring them to God in prayer by name, and ask for help to forgive, even if the feeling has not caught up yet.
11.prayer: Thank God that Jesus came as a humble king who welcomes all nations. Ask him to show you where your life looks full of leaves but short on fruit, and to help you pray and forgive with honest trust.
11.tip: Verses 23 and 24 can sound like a promise that prayer always gets us what we ask, which can wound people who have prayed hard and not received. Let people say so honestly. Gently point to the surrounding call to trust God and to forgive, and avoid giving quick answers.

12.open: When have you been put on the spot with a question you did not know how to answer?
questions: In the story the owner keeps sending servants, and at last sends "one beloved son" (v. 6). What does this tell you about the owner, and about the tenants?
The leaders knew "He had spoken this parable against them" (v. 12). Why can it be so hard to hear a truth that lands close to home? When has that happened to you?

Verse 9 says the owner will "give the vineyard to others." Christians differ on whether this means God turning from Israel as a people to the church, or God removing the particular leaders who rejected Jesus. What do you notice in the story that shapes how you read it?
Jesus asks, "Whose image is this? And whose inscription?" (v. 16) and then says to give "to God what is God's" (v. 17). What do you think belongs to God, and how do you give it?
Jesus says God "is not the God of the dead, but of the living" (v. 27). What do you hope, wonder or struggle with when you think about life after death? Honest doubts are welcome here.
Jesus says to "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength" (v. 30). Which of those four is hardest for you right now, and why?
Jesus tells the scribe, "You are not far from the kingdom of God" (v. 34). What do you think it looks like to be near but not yet in? What might the next step be?

Jesus says the widow "out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on" (v. 44). What stands out to you about how Jesus measures a gift? How does that change the way you think about what you have to offer?
12.life: This week, pick one person and do one small, concrete act of love that costs you something, like time, comfort or money. Afterward, notice how it felt to give that way.
12.prayer: Ask God to help you love him with all that you are, and to show you one neighbor to love this week. Pray for anyone in the group who feels they have little to give.
12.tip: The vineyard parable has sometimes been used unfairly against Jewish people, so say gently that Jesus and his first followers were Jewish and that his target here is the leaders. Then mention that Christians read 'to others' in different ways, and move on without settling it.

13.open: Is there a building, a place or an object you've seen that made you think, 'that will surely last forever'?
questions: A disciple says, "Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!" (v. 1). Jesus answers that "not one stone here will be left on another" (v. 2). What do you think the disciples felt hearing that, and why?
Jesus begins with, "See to it that no one deceives you" (v. 5). Where do voices claiming to speak for Jesus or about the future show up today, and how do you sort through them?

Jesus says wars and earthquakes are "the beginning of birth pains" and tells them "do not be alarmed" (vv. 7, 8). Why might he say that about frightening news? What helps you when the headlines feel heavy?

He warns that his followers will face trials, and even betrayal by family, yet "the one who perseveres to the end will be saved" (v. 13). What do you think it looks like to hold on, especially when you are tired or unsure?
In verse 11 he says, "do not worry beforehand what to say," because the Holy Spirit will give the words. When have you felt tongue-tied about your faith, and what would it mean to trust that promise?

Verse 32 says, "No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father." How does it feel to be told that you will not be given a timetable? Be honest if it frustrates you or if it comes as a relief.

Jesus ends with, "Keep watch!" (v. 37), and the servants in his story each have a task (v. 34). What would it look like to stay alert and faithful in ordinary work this week, rather than anxious or asleep?
Our study note asks: what in your life feels as solid as those temple stones, and what would be left if it fell? How might your answer shape what you hold onto?
13.life: Pick one ordinary task you have been given, at home, work, church or in your neighborhood, and do it this week as though Jesus might check in on it. Then, when the news feels overwhelming, turn it off for a while and pray instead.
13.prayer: Ask God for a steady heart when the world feels shaky. Pray for anyone in the group who is facing pressure or fear, and ask for the grace to stay awake and faithful.
13.tip: This chapter draws lots of timeline questions, and Christians differ on what was fulfilled in AD 70 and what is still ahead. Say that plainly in a sentence, then steer the group back to what Jesus stresses: do not be deceived, do not panic, keep watch. If someone pushes prediction charts, thank them and return to verse 32.

14.open: Think of a meal you still remember years later. Who was there, and what made it stick?
questions: The woman breaks open an expensive jar and pours it on Jesus, and some "scolded her" (v. 5). Jesus calls it "a beautiful deed" (v. 6). Why do you think people reacted so differently to the same act?
Jesus says of her, "She has done what she could" (v. 8). What does that phrase say about what God asks of us? Where do you feel you have very little to offer?

At the table Jesus says one of them will betray him, and each disciple asks, "Surely not I?" (v. 19). Why might all twelve have wondered about themselves? What does that tell us about how well we know our own hearts?
Jesus takes the bread and says, "Take it; this is My body" (v. 22). What do you think the disciples understood in that room, and what does the meal mean to you today?
Peter says, "Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You" (v. 31), and the others "said the same thing." Why do we make promises like that, and what happens when we cannot keep them?

In Gethsemane Jesus prays, "Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will" (v. 36). What strikes you about Jesus asking for another way? When have you prayed something like that, or found it hard to?

Jesus finds his friends asleep and says, "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (v. 38). He does not walk away from them. What does that show you about how he sees our weakness? If you honestly feel distant from God or unsure about any of this, what is that like for you right now?
After Peter denies Jesus the third time, "he broke down and wept" (v. 72). What do you think Peter felt in that moment, and what hope can we hold onto for people who have failed?
14.life: Think of someone you have let down, or who has let you down. This week, take one small step toward them, such as a call, a note or a shared meal. Before you do, tell God honestly where you have fallen short too.
14.prayer: Thank Jesus for staying faithful when his friends fell asleep and ran. Ask him to help you be honest about your weakness and trust his strength.
14.tip: Many people will want to talk about what Jesus meant by "this is My body" in verse 22. Say in one line that Christians differ here: some believe Jesus is truly present in the bread and wine, and others see the meal as a symbol and remembrance. Then bring the group back to what the meal meant that night, and to Peter's story, which many people find the most personal part.

15.open: Think of a time you were in a crowd that went along with something. What made it hard or easy to go along?
questions: Pilate asks if Jesus is the King of the Jews, and Jesus answers, "You have said so" (v. 2). Then Jesus makes "no further reply" (v. 5). Why might he choose silence, and what do you make of it?

Pilate knew "it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over" (v. 10), yet he gave in anyway, "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (v. 15). When have you seen someone know better and still go along?
When a crowd turns against someone, what helps you tell whether the crowd is right? How might you stand apart from a crowd without being harsh toward it?

The soldiers say, "Hail, King of the Jews!" as a joke (v. 18), and the sign above the cross reads "THE KING OF THE JEWS" (v. 26). Mark seems to see something true in the mockery. What kind of king do you see in this scene?

Simon of Cyrene was made to carry the cross of Jesus when the soldiers grabbed him as he was passing by (v. 21). He never asked for it. Have you ever been pulled into something hard that you did not choose? What was that like?

Jesus cries, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (v. 34). Christians read this differently: some believe God truly turned away as Jesus bore the world's sin, and others hear Jesus praying the opening of Psalm 22, holding on to trust in agony. Whichever way you lean, what do you do with a prayer that sounds this raw? If you have ever felt that God was far away, how did you say so, if you did?
The centurion, a Roman soldier, says, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (v. 39). What do you think he saw in how Jesus died that moved him?
The women watched "from a distance" (v. 40), and Joseph "boldly" asked for the body (v. 43). Which of these two do you identify with more right now, and why?
15.life: This week, think of one person who is being left out or talked about unfairly. Do one small, kind thing for them, such as a message, a seat beside them, or a good word said in their defense.
15.prayer: Thank Jesus for staying faithful all the way to the cross. Ask God for honesty when you feel far from him, and for courage to stand with the person others are turning on.
15.tip: Verse 34 can stir up real doubt and pain, so do not rush to explain it away. Mention in one line that Christians read it differently, then let people say how it lands for them. It is fine to leave it unresolved and simply stay with the question.

16.open: Tell about a time you got surprising news and didn't know what to do with it.
questions: The women worried about who would "roll away the stone" (v. 3), yet found it already moved. What is a stone in your life right now that you keep worrying about?
The women came to anoint a dead body, not to meet a living Lord. Why do you think they were not expecting Jesus to rise, even though he had told them?
The messenger says, "He has risen! He is not here!" (v. 6). Why does it matter to the Christian faith that the tomb was empty and not only that Jesus' memory lived on?
The message is for "His disciples and Peter" (v. 7). Peter had denied knowing Jesus. What does it say about God that Peter is named on purpose?

The women ran away "trembling and bewildered," and "did not say a word to anyone" (v. 8). What do you make of the story ending, in the oldest copies, with fear and silence? How might you have reacted?

Verses 11 and 13 say the other followers "did not believe it." Jesus meets that doubt with a rebuke in verse 14, yet he still stays with them and sends them out. What do you notice about how he treats people who struggle to believe? Where are you honestly unsure right now?
Jesus says, "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature" (v. 15). What would sharing good news look like in your own everyday life, without it feeling forced?

Verses 9 to 20 are missing from the earliest copies, and Christians differ on how to treat them, especially the signs in verses 17 and 18. How can we read this part carefully and humbly, and what in it is clear and encouraging to you?
16.life: This week, think of one person who may feel they have failed or are left out, as Peter might have. Send them a kind message or invite them for coffee, and let them know they are welcome.
16.prayer: Thank God that Jesus is risen and that the stone was moved. Ask for honesty about your doubts and fears, and for courage to share good news this week.
16.tip: Verses 17 and 18 about snakes and poison can take over the whole evening. Say once, plainly, that Christians read this ending differently and that it is missing from the earliest copies, then steer back to the empty tomb, Peter being named, and Jesus' patience with doubt.
